assessment.nobel_worthiness: Changed how economists and policymakers understand technology, trade exposure and labour-market adjustment. The China-shock work and the task-based approach link new local-labour-market data to credible causal designs. The findings on persistent regional and worker-level losses bear directly on how societies handle structural change.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock evidence is most clearly credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson as a trio. The task framework has other originators who are not on this ballot's list, so the proposal is limited to the trade-shock core. Katz is credited here, but his main recognition rests on the broader skills-versus-technology literature.
assessment.maturity: Core papers date from about 2013 to 2016 and have been replicated, extended and debated for a decade. The literature is mature enough to judge, and it is still active.
uncertainties: The task-model originators are not on the credited list, so the attribution split is imperfect.
Debate continues over the long-run size of the trade-shock effects and over whether the China shock is a special episode.
The overlap with recent prizes on technology and growth is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Built long-run historical series of top incomes and wealth from tax records. This changed the empirical basis of research on distribution, taxation and capitalism. It is archive-driven dataset construction paired with sustained analysis, and it opened a large research field.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez started the top-income series and their international extension. Zucman's offshore-wealth and distributional national accounts work is influential but more recent, so he is left out of the proposal. Many co-authors and collaborators contributed to the World Inequality Database.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from the early 2000s and has been confirmed and refined by many countries' series. The methodological debates are well developed.
uncertainties: Some measurement choices, such as the treatment of capital income and the capital-share findings, remain contested.
Policy advocacy may colour how the committee reads the scholarship.
Whether to include Zucman is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Brought electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal policy into the core of economics using formal models tied to empirical tests. This created the modern field of political economics, with wide influence on comparative politics and public economics. I note a possible link to my own cross-disciplinary collaboration with political scientists.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central figures in the constitutional and electoral-rule research programme. Besley's work on state capacity and on accountability is closely related and often joint with Persson. The three-person grouping is coherent.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of work have been tested empirically and cited extensively. Recent prize recognition of institutions may be seen as overlapping.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity may reduce the appetite for this adjacent area.
Whether Besley's contribution is judged equal to the other two is unclear.
Some empirical results on constitutions are sensitive to identification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The collateral-constraint model of credit cycles explains how small shocks are amplified through asset prices and borrowing limits. It is foundational for macro-finance and became highly relevant after the 2008 crisis. It is a clear theoretical contribution with a wide empirical follow-up literature.
assessment.attribution: The 1997 Kiyotaki and Moore paper is the clear origin of the mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist developed the financial-accelerator and empirical strands, but Bernanke, the third originator of the accelerator, was already recognised in 2022, so the proposal is limited to Kiyotaki and Moore.
assessment.maturity: Almost thirty years of use in theory and policy models. The idea is well established.
uncertainties: The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises may be read as overlapping.
The relative weight of Gertler, Gilchrist and Bernanke in the accelerator tradition is uncertain.
Direct empirical identification of the amplification channel is mixed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed international trade theory and the measurement of gains from trade, and made firm-level micro-data central to the field. It follows the 2008 prize for new trade theory and extends it in a major way.
assessment.attribution: Melitz's 2003 model is the central breakthrough. Helpman contributed heavily to the wider firm-level trade agenda and to the theory behind it. Redding's contributions are significant, particularly in quantitative spatial models, but they come later and are less central here.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation with firm-level data. The framework is standard in graduate teaching.
uncertainties: Partial overlap with the 2008 prize for new trade theory.
Helpman's role may also be assessed under B029 (trade politics).
Some of the quantitative gains-from-trade results depend on the model structure.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Used population-scale administrative data to measure intergenerational mobility and its local variation. This transformed the empirical study of opportunity and neighbourhood effects. The data construction is large-scale and the methods are rigorous, and the work influenced policy debates.
assessment.attribution: Chetty led the mobility atlas work with many co-authors. Hendren is central to the work on place effects and the Opportunity Atlas. Friedman and Katz contributed substantial shares, but credit is spread widely across a large team.
assessment.maturity: The core results date from about 2014 to 2022. Replication and long-run follow-up are still developing, so the case is likely to strengthen with time.
uncertainties: Chetty's work spans other topics such as taxation and tax-policy evaluation, and the committee would need to decide the exact scope.
Concerns about the causal interpretation of place effects.
Maturity is lower than for other candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework quantifies how frictions that distort input allocation across firms can explain a large part of cross-country income differences. It links micro-data to aggregate productivity and brought structure to the study of development gaps.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow's 2009 paper is the key contribution. Restuccia and Rogerson developed a parallel approach, and Rogerson is not on this list. Restuccia is credited but his role is complementary, so the proposal is limited to Hsieh and Klenow.
assessment.maturity: Fifteen or more years of use. The measurement approach has been applied widely, though its methodological limits are well known.
uncertainties: Measurement error in firm-level data may drive part of the measured misallocation.
The attribution to Restuccia and Rogerson is unresolved.
Overlap with other growth-related recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model is a canonical non-cooperative treatment of negotiation, with a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium. It shaped the theory of markets, labour negotiation and political bargaining. It is a durable and elegant theoretical contribution.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein's 1982 paper is the central result. Wolinsky co-developed bargaining in markets, and Binmore contributed to the strategic foundations and to the Nash programme. Rubinstein alone is the cleanest attribution.
assessment.maturity: More than forty years of use. A long gap since publication means the standing is fully established, though prize timing may reflect other game-theory recognition.
uncertainties: Earlier prizes recognised related game-theory work, so the field may be viewed as already rewarded.
Whether to include Wolinsky and Binmore is unclear.
Applied and empirical impact is narrower than for several other candidates.
